analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and senior officials from owning or trading individual stocks and severely curbs the lobbying revolving door.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 6 cosponsors and referred to ten House committees, received no committee action or vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This wide-ranging ethics bill would bar members of Congress, cabinet secretaries, federal judges, and other senior officials from owning or trading individual stocks or serving on corporate boards, impose long cooling-off periods before former officials can lobby, and create an independent agency to enforce federal ethics laws. It would also require presidents, vice presidents, members, and candidates to release tax returns, ban corporate PAC money, and create small-dollar public financing for Senate and presidential campaigns. It was referred to ten committees, none of which acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary citizens would gain tighter limits on conflicts of interest in government: lawmakers and senior officials could no longer hold or trade individual stocks that their own decisions could move, the revolving door between government and lobbying firms would narrow sharply, and an independent Office of Public Integrity would enforce ethics rules that are now largely policed by the officials' own parties and agencies. Candidates reliant on small donations would get public matching funds, reducing dependence on corporate PACs and large donors.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress, cabinet secretaries, federal judges, and other senior government officials from owning or trading individual stock or serving on corporate boards, while allowing diversified widely held funds and a conflict-free federal investment account [S2] [S3].

Bans lobbying by former members of Congress, presidents, and agency heads, with 2-year bans for registered lobbyists and 6-year bans for corporate lobbyists moving into government jobs, and bars giant banks and large federal contractors from hiring senior officials for four years after they leave office [S2] [S3].
Requires the Supreme Court to follow the ethics rules that bind all other federal judges and creates a new, independent anti-corruption agency dedicated to enforcing federal ethics laws [S2].

Requires presidents, vice presidents, members of Congress, and candidates to disclose tax returns and more financial information, and increases disclosure of the corporate money behind lobbying [S2] [S3].

Bans corporate PAC contributions to members of Congress, bars super PAC-candidate coordination, restricts big-donor ambassador appointments, and creates small-dollar public financing for Senate and presidential campaigns [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, members of Congress and other senior officials would have to divest individual stocks, disclose tax returns, and give up post-government lobbying careers they can currently pursue after short cooling-off periods. Lobbying firms, large banks, and federal contractors would lose a hiring pipeline of former officials and face new disclosure rules, and taxpayers would fund the new enforcement agency and the public financing system.

drawbacks.text: The stock and securities ban reaches well beyond Congress: it covers any executive-branch employee at the GS-15 level or higher and other senior officials, which could complicate recruiting and retaining experienced professionals in fields like finance, health, and science who hold individual securities [S3].

The multi-year lobbying and post-employment bans are sweeping, and critics of such restrictions have long argued they raise First Amendment concerns and risk pushing influence work into less visible, unregistered channels rather than eliminating it [S3].

The bill creates a new Office of Public Integrity with broad enforcement power and authorizes unspecified appropriations for it and for public campaign financing, adding new government spending and a powerful new bureaucracy [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core conflict-of-interest provisions go after a real and well-documented problem: lawmakers and senior officials trading stocks their own decisions can move, and moving into lobbying jobs that trade on their government access. The costs are real but manageable in kind: the broadest definitions sweep in mid-career federal employees who pose little corruption risk, the enforcement agency concentrates significant power in a new body, and public financing costs money. The trade-off favors passage on the merits, but the bill's breadth made it easy for committees to defer action and never had to be defended in a markup.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 116th Congress and referred to ten committees, none of which took it up, so it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Anti-Corruption and Public Integrity Act on December 18, 2020, with Reps. Norton, Sarbanes, Omar, and Schakowsky as original cosponsors [S3].

The same day, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee and nine other committees: Oversight and Reform, House Administration, Ways and Means, Financial Services, Intelligence, Rules, Foreign Affairs, Armed Services, and Budget [S5].
No committee acted on the bill and it never received a floor vote; its only cosponsors were 6 House Democrats [S4] [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired without any action beyond referral [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and senior officials keep the ability to own and trade individual stocks and to move into lobbying after short cooling-off periods, and the lobbying firms, banks, and contractors that hire them keep the revolving door as it is. Because the bill died without a vote, no one had to defend or oppose any of its provisions on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent officials and the lobbying industry

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats supported the bill (one sponsor and 6 cosponsors, all Democrats), no Republican backed it, and because it never reached a floor vote no one had to vote for or against it on the record.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and corporate lobbying departments
industries.note: The bill would impose a lifetime ban on lobbying by former members of Congress, presidents, and agency heads, 6-year cooling-off periods for corporate lobbyists entering government, a progressive tax on lobbying expenditures, and new disclosure requirements. The industry's business model depends on the revolving door and relationships this bill targets.

industries.industry: Large banks, federal contractors, and major corporations
industries.note: Giant banks and companies would be barred from hiring senior officials for four years after they leave government, companies under federal enforcement actions could not place executives in agencies for six years, and contractors would have to disclose political spending. Their interest in continued access to former officials runs against the public's interest in independent procurement and regulation.

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders (members of Congress and senior officials)
industries.note: They would have to divest individual stocks, serve on no corporate boards, disclose tax returns, and give up lucrative post-office lobbying careers. The people whose conduct would be regulated were the ones whose committees controlled the bill's fate.

industries.industry: Think tanks, tax-exempt nonprofits, and online political advertisers
industries.note: The bill would require disclosure of funding behind policy advocacy and extend election advertising disclaimers and political record requirements to online platforms, reducing channels for unattributed influence spending.
